al_brandnewbia.blurb: A steep sandstone sport wall in Little River Canyon, northeast Alabama. The climbing is hard: the bulk of the routes fall in the 5.12 range, with a good number of 5.11s and only a couple of 5.10s, so it suits climbers comfortable well past the moderate grades. Quality is uneven, with some seepage and patches of dull rock, but the best lines are well rated, and it tends to be quieter than the canyon's busier walls. The wall collects plenty of sun, so cooler days are kinder. Most lines need a few days to dry after heavy rain, though a handful sit under overhangs and stay dry sooner.

al_deck_area_front_slabs.blurb: A group of sandstone boulders near the front of Horse Pens 40, the well-known bouldering park on Chandler Mountain in St. Clair County. The problems here cover nearly the whole range, from VB and V0 warm-ups up through V7 and V8, with the middle grades well represented, so a mixed group can find something. Hammerhead, Earth Wind & Fire, Night Fever and Alabama Tiller are among the favorites. The sandstone is known for slopers, and some of the rock is soft, so expect friction-dependent moves and tricky mantles and top-outs. Fall through spring is the most comfortable season.

al_roadside_crag.blurb: A small, easy-to-reach cliff in the Southwest section of Buck's Pocket, in northeast Alabama. It is mostly sport climbing with a few trad lines, and the grades lean friendly: most routes are between 5.6 and 5.10, with a few harder ones above. King Boo and Trail Boss, both 5.9, are standouts. The routes often start on a pebbly base before moving onto sandstone, and the wall has some broken, discontinuous features. It sits close to the road and is shaded for most of the day, which makes it a pleasant summer stop and a reasonable place for newer leaders. The park is remote, so cell service is thin.
al_roadside_crag.parking_note: Use the big curved pull-off beside the road; a trail climbs up and to the left from there to the base of the cliff.

ak_mineral_creek_ice_climbs_2.blurb: A canyon of frozen waterfalls just outside Valdez, in the wet maritime climate of Prince William Sound. The ice spans the range, from easy WI2 and WI3 flows through a strong middle of WI4 and WI5, up to a couple of WI6 lines, and Wowie Zowie is the headline two-pitch classic. The valley carries high avalanche danger, so judge the slopes above the climbs carefully before committing. Ice around Valdez generally forms from early winter and is at its best around late February. Reaching the main climbs is simple, since they are visible from the trail up the valley.
ak_mineral_creek_ice_climbs_2.approach: Follow the Mineral Creek Trail, cross the metal bridge, and keep going a short distance up the main trail. The main climbs show on the east (right) side of the valley. Farther routes continue up the snowmachine track.

ak_left_side_walls.blurb: The left-hand section of the Wookie Wall at Weiner Lake, off the Glenn Highway between Palmer and Chickaloon, in a part of Alaska with very little bolted rock climbing. The cliff is steep and overhanging, formed of big stacked pillars, and the climbing is powerful, with cracks, slopers, edges and pockets. Routes here are a near even split of sport and trad, mostly 5.10 through 5.12 with a couple of 5.13s. Pumpkin Party, Higher Calling and The Last Wookie are well-liked sport lines. The wall holds sun late into the day, so it is best in the cool shoulder seasons; in summer, climb mornings or evenings. Weekends draw a crowd.

ab_lower_wall_2.blurb: The first wall you reach on the trail to Acéphale, a limestone sport crag on the flank of Heart Mountain above the Bow Valley. This is hard climbing on slopey edges: the great majority of routes are 5.12 or 5.13, with only a handful at 5.11 or below. Deal With It and Nemo are among the better known. It sits among trees and stays shaded, so it can be cool, and there is some road noise from the highway. The walk is steep but among the shorter in the valley, and the wall draws a steady crowd on good days.
ab_lower_wall_2.parking_note: Drive toward Calgary from Canmore, past the Lac des Arcs exit, to a guardrail about 2 km on; turn right into the wide dirt pull-out.
ab_lower_wall_2.approach: A steep signed trail climbs from the pull-out through the forest to the base of the first wall.

ab_atlantis_wall.blurb: A limestone sport wall in the Lookout section of Echo Canyon, above Canmore. The grades run hard: roughly equal numbers of 5.12 and 5.13, a scattering of 5.14, and very little below 5.12. Fresh Prince and Atlantis are two of the prominent lines. The Lookout takes a lot of sun, which makes it lovely in fall and on clear winter days but hot in midsummer, and it fills up on weekends. The canyon's rock is consistent in quality, and the area is popular with climbers from both Canmore and Calgary.
ab_atlantis_wall.parking_note: Park on Indian Flats Road below the Canmore hostel.
ab_atlantis_wall.approach: Walk up the road to the Grotto Mountain trailhead, wind through the forest to a creek bed, and follow it upstream; the Lookout trail leaves the creek just beyond a big blocky boulder on the left.

ab_yellow_wall_barrier_wall.blurb: The most popular wall at Barrier Bluffs, a limestone crag on Mount Baldy above Barrier Lake in Kananaskis. It is mostly sport, with a few trad lines, and the climbing sits squarely in the 5.11 range, with a decent supply of 5.9 and 5.10 and a few 5.12s. The rock is good, the approach is short, and the area has been a regional favorite for decades, so expect company on weekends. Sisyphus Goes to Hollywood and Requiem are two of the stand-out lines. Newer crags nearby continue to add harder routes.
ab_yellow_wall_barrier_wall.parking_note: Take Highway 40 south from the TransCanada toward Barrier Lake and use the roadside pull-out on the east side just beyond the lake.
ab_yellow_wall_barrier_wall.approach: A clear climbers' trail leads steeply uphill, staying close to the left of the drainage. At the cliff, most routes are to the right.

ab_3_saddle_up_wall.blurb: A tier of the Coliseum in Echo Canyon above Canmore, and a wall for strong sport climbers. The rock is limestone and the routes are almost all 5.12 or 5.13, with the largest group at 5.13 and a couple of 5.14s and a 5.15 above that. Almost nothing here is below 5.11, so it is not a place to warm up from scratch. The canyon's stone is consistent in quality, the area was developed fairly recently, and it attracts climbers from both Canmore and Calgary.
ab_3_saddle_up_wall.parking_note: Park on Indian Flats Road below the Canmore hostel.
ab_3_saddle_up_wall.approach: Walk up to the Grotto Mountain trailhead and follow the forest trail to the creek bed. Stay in the creek past the small rock steps, then take the trail on the left roughly 50 m beyond them to reach the Coliseum.

ab_moose_patch.blurb: A limestone sport and trad crag on Moose Mountain in the Kananaskis front ranges, west of Calgary. Routes are around 25 to 30 meters and the grades are concentrated in the 5.11s, with a few 5.10s and 5.12s, so it suits climbers who have moved past the moderate grades. Rock quality varies from marginal in places to very good, and most routes are well starred. The wall is shaded until mid or late morning and then gets full sun, and it can be breezy. Moose Mountain's crags generally stay climbable well into spring and fall.
ab_moose_patch.approach: Follow the Moose Mountain road to the first crag on your right, then continue about 300 m and look for a signed trail leading uphill to the right; it brings you into the middle of Moose Patch.
